**February 29, 1960 — a Monday**

Before anything else: the date itself. February 29 exists only because the Earth takes approximately 365.25 days to orbit the sun, and the calendar has to correct for the accumulating fraction. You were born on the correction day — one of roughly 4.5 million people alive today who share it. In 66 years, you have had 16 actual February 29 birthdays. The next one is 2028, when you'll be 68. By strict calendar count, you age at one quarter the rate of everyone else.

It's a birthday that forces a small philosophical question every non-leap year: what day do you actually turn? February 28 or March 1? The law in most countries splits on this. You've been navigating the ambiguity your entire life.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, the city of Agadir, Morocco was destroyed.

At 11:47 PM local time on February 29, an earthquake struck. Agadir was a modern coastal city — rebuilt after an earlier quake in the 1930s — and much of it collapsed within seconds. Roughly 12,000 to 15,000 people died, a third of the city's population. The Moroccan government eventually bulldozed the ruins and rebuilt the city from scratch a few kilometers away. Agadir today sits beside the memory of the city that existed when you were born.

It's a dark coincidence and a significant one: one of the deadliest earthquakes in African history fell on the rarest date in the Western calendar.

---

**Four weeks before your birth**, on February 1, four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina and refused to leave. By February 29 — the day you arrived — the Greensboro sit-ins had already spread. Students in other cities were organizing, the national press was paying attention, and the tactic of nonviolent direct action was proving its power. The civil rights movement was entering its most concentrated decade of direct confrontation, and it was already in motion on the morning you were born.

---

**1960 was a hinge year**, and you entered at its beginning.

In May, an American U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union. Francis Gary Powers was captured, and Eisenhower was caught in a lie about the mission. The Paris summit collapsed. The Cold War, which had briefly seemed to be softening, hardened again.

In May as well, the FDA approved the oral contraceptive pill — arguably the most consequential regulatory decision of the postwar era. The social changes that followed, over the next two decades, were as profound as any technology of the century.

In November, John F. Kennedy defeated Richard Nixon by one of the narrowest margins in American history. The Eisenhower era — the world you were born into — ended before you were nine months old. Kennedy's presidency lasted three years.

And in 1960, seventeen African nations gained independence. The colonial map of Africa, which had been largely fixed since the late 19th century, was dissolving in a single year. The "Wind of Change," as British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan had called it in a speech just 26 days before your birth, was blowing faster than even he anticipated.

---

**The arc of 66 years**

You were born in the last months of the Eisenhower presidency, into a world that felt stable in ways it was already ceasing to be. You were three when Kennedy was shot. Nine when Apollo 11 landed on the moon. You came of age during Vietnam and Watergate — formative experiences for everyone who was a teenager in the early 1970s, but particularly sharp for a generation that had watched the idealism of the early 60s curdle.

You were 29 when the Berlin Wall fell, young enough that it still felt astonishing rather than inevitable. You were 41 on September 11. The digital revolution ran through your working life — you were old enough to remember offices without computers, young enough to adapt to everything that came after.

The world you entered on that February 29 had no interstate highway system yet completed, no birth control pill, no manned space program, a colonial Africa, and a Soviet empire that everyone assumed was permanent. By the time you've had your 17th birthday in 2028, you'll have outlived the Berlin Wall by nearly 40 years.

You were born on a day that recurs only once every four years, in a year that changed more than most, on the very night a city disappeared. It's an unusual beginning to an unusual span of time.
